title: Ganesh Chaturthi (the clay idol; the immersion)
hook: after days as a guest, Ganesha is carried to the water, and the crowd asks him to come back sooner next year
carry: Ganesh Chaturthi (the clay idol; the immersion)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ganesh Chaturthi: the clay Ganesha carried home, invited in, and treated as a guest. Did you clear a space? Today, the hard part: letting him go. And a look back at the week. Day one hundred forty-seven.

It's the last day. The Ganesha who's been sitting in the living room, fed and sung to, is lifted off his seat. The family does one last arti. Then out the door, into a street that's become a river of people: drums, dancing, colored powder, Ganesha after Ganesha moving slowly toward the sea. At the shore, people wade in up to their waists and lower him into the water. He slips under. And the whole beach shouts the same thing: Ganpati Bappa Morya, pudhchya varshi lavkar ya. Father Ganesha, come early next year. A lot of people are crying.
screen: `ONE LAST ARTI.` → `A RIVER OF PEOPLE TO THE SEA.` → `COME EARLY NEXT YEAR.`

segments.voice: The immersion is called visarjan, from a Sanskrit root that means to let go, to release. It happens on different days in different homes: after a day and a half, or three, five, seven, and the biggest crowds on Anant Chaturdashi, ten days after Chaturthi. So why make a god from clay, give him a room, feed him for days, and then drown him? Here's how many Hindus explain it. The clay image was never the whole of Ganesha. He was invited into it, and now he's sent off, back to wherever he's always been. The clay goes back to the water and the earth it came from. What was shaped by hand is unshaped again. Nothing is kept. And that's the practice hiding in the festival: welcome something fully, and then let it go fully. The clay image isn't kept on a shelf for fear of losing it. The goodbye is part of the love. There's an honest problem in the modern festival too. Many big images are made of plaster and painted with chemical colors, and they don't dissolve; they pile up in rivers and the sea. So many families have gone back to plain clay, sometimes immersing their Ganesha in a bucket at home and pouring the water on the garden. The old form turns out to be the kinder one. And this week, look what you've walked through. Holi's fire and colors. Navaratri's nine faces and nine nights. Janmashtami's midnight cradle. Ganesha arriving, and leaving. Four festivals. Each one a way of living a story with your hands.
screen: `VISARJAN: TO LET GO.` · `THE CLAY GOES BACK TO THE WATER.` · `WELCOME FULLY, RELEASE FULLY.` · `THE WEEK: FIRE, NIGHTS, CRADLE, CLAY.` · then, large: `THE GOODBYE IS PART OF THE LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: carry him to the water. Settle, and breathe. Picture the Ganesha you welcomed yesterday, sitting in the space you cleared. Now think of one thing in your life that's had its season: a plan that's done, a role you've outgrown, a worry you've been hosting. Set it in his lap. Lift him up. Walk slowly, with the drums, to the water's edge. Wade in. Lower him gently, and let go. Watch the water close. If you like, say it with the crowd, silently: come again next year. The bell holds the time.
Ganesh Chaturthi. He arrives in clay on the fourth day, stays as a guest, and is given back to the water, with a promise to come again.
Your line: Ganesh Chaturthi, the clay idol, the immersion. Today, finish one goodbye properly: return the borrowed thing, close the old tab, say thank you for a season. Day one hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: At the end of Ganesh Chaturthi, after one and a half to ten days, many Hindus perform a final arti and carry the clay Ganesha in procession to a river, lake or the sea for visarjan, chanting Ganpati Bappa Morya; many now use plain clay or immerse at home.

fork.setup: your family's Ganesha has been with you for days. the kids love him. it's the last day. what do you do?

fork.reveal: one last arti, a procession, and the water. the goodbye is part of the festival, and the crowd asks him to come early next year.

original.note: Sanskrit: letting go, release. the immersion that ends the festival.

trapdoor: what you thought: throwing a statue in the sea.
what it means: a guest sent home. he was invited into the clay, and the clay goes back to the water it came from.
what a scholar hears: visarjan, from a root meaning to release. plaster images that don't dissolve have pushed many families back to plain clay.

notes: Marathi chant 'Ganpati Bappa Morya, pudhchya varshi lavkar ya' ('come early next year'). Confirm transliteration.
Immersion days: 1.5, 3, 5, 7, 10 (Anant Chaturdashi, the 14th tithi, ten days after Chaturthi). Confirm.
The explanation (the image as a temporary seat of a presence that is then released) is common but not universal. Framed as 'how many Hindus explain it'. Confirm.
'Visarjan' from vi + srj, to release/let go. Confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): Anant Chaturdashi is the fourteenth lunar day, ten days after Chaturthi (the eleventh day counted inclusively), so 'the tenth day, called Anant Chaturdashi' became 'Anant Chaturdashi, ten days after Chaturthi' in the teach, match and myth. 'A thousand Ganeshas' (an invented count) cut. 'Don't keep the image on a shelf' (the narrator instructing) became a description.
